title: Bentkus-type asymptotic e-values
claim: Bound functions with larger tuning parameter attain lower minima near the ideal threshold, and the gap to it shrinks as confidence level tightens.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared legend in first panel, dashed baseline
description: Three side-by-side line plots, one for each confidence level delta = 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001, with titles above each panel. The x-axis is lambda from 0 to 6, and the y-axis is sqrt(n) R_n, with the range shifting upward from panel to panel. Each panel has seven colored curves for U_{delta,alpha} with alpha from 0 to 5 plus infinity. Gray is alpha=0, blue 1, cyan 2, green 3, magenta 4, brown 5 and orange infinity. A black dashed horizontal line marks the target level z_delta. The curves are U-shaped. Each has a different minimum, and they converge into one rising branch at large lambda. The orange infinity curve is flatter and crosses the others. A legend sits in the upper right of the left panel. The eye goes first to the colorful crossing curves near their minima.
caption: Evaluation of Uδ,∞(λ) and Uδ,α(λ) for α ∈{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and δ ∈{0.1, 0.01, 0.001}.
abstract: Asymptotic e-values are emerging as a powerful alternative to asymptotic p-values, particularly in post-hoc inference and multiple testing, where significance levels may be data-dependent. Existing asymptotic e-values, however, suffer from the ``missing factor,'' a scaling inefficiency resulting in overly conservative inference. Drawing on the framework of near-optimal concentration inequalities developed by Bentkus in the 2000s, we introduce Bentkus-type asymptotic e-values and prove that they successfully eliminate the missing factor. We also demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that Bentkus-type e-values consistently deliver sharper inference than existing alternatives, leading to tighter post-hoc confidence intervals and higher rejection rates in multiple testing procedures.
